questions.question: On a bar graph, one square stands for 5 cookies. A bar is 6 squares tall. How many cookies does that bar show?
questions.explain: With many-to-one correspondence you multiply: 6 squares × 5 cookies = 30 cookies. The common trap is adding (6 + 5 = 11) or just counting the squares (6) as if one square meant one cookie.

questions.question: The scale on a bar graph is marked 0, 10, 20, 30, 40. One bar ends exactly halfway between 30 and 40. What number does that bar show?
questions.explain: Each space on the scale is worth 10, so halfway up a space is worth 5: 30 + 5 = 35. The trap is rounding down to the line below (30) or up to the line above (40) instead of using half of the scale value.

questions.question: A graph shows how many books each class read. Which statement tells you the graph uses MANY-TO-ONE correspondence?
options: Each square on the graph stands for exactly 1 book.
Every bar on the graph is the same height.
Each square on the graph stands for 10 books.
The graph shows two bars side by side for each month.
questions.explain: Many-to-one means one symbol or square stands for a group of things, such as 1 square = 10 books. If one square stands for exactly 1 book that is one-to-one correspondence, and having two bars side by side only tells you it is a double bar graph.

questions.question: On a bar graph, one square stands for 5 cookies. How tall must a bar be to show 45 cookies?
questions.explain: To go from the real amount back to squares you divide: 45 ÷ 5 = 9 squares. The trap is drawing 45 squares (treating one square as one cookie) or subtracting 45 − 5 instead of dividing.

questions.question: Division 5 and Division 6 collected bottles for a school trip. On the double bar graph, one square stands for 20 bottles. Division 5's bar is 7 squares tall and Division 6's bar is 4 squares tall. How many bottles did the two divisions collect altogether?
questions.explain: Change each bar to real bottles first, then add: 7 × 20 = 140 and 4 × 20 = 80, so 140 + 80 = 220 bottles. The trap is adding the squares (7 + 4 = 11) and forgetting that each square is worth 20.

questions.question: Emma is drawing a bar graph on grid paper that is only 10 squares tall. Her largest amount is 90 rainy days. Which scale should she choose?
questions.explain: Pick a scale so the biggest value fits the grid: 90 ÷ 10 = 9 squares, so 10 days per square works. Using 1 day per square would need a bar 90 squares tall, and 100 days per square would squash every bar into less than one square.

questions.question: A double bar graph shows bake-sale money, and one square stands for $25. Saturday's bar is 6 squares tall and Sunday's bar is 9 squares tall. How much MORE money was raised on Sunday than on Saturday?
questions.explain: Find the difference in squares and then multiply by the scale: 9 − 6 = 3 squares, and 3 × $25 = $75. The trap is answering $3 (the square difference, with no scale) or $225, which is all of Sunday's money instead of the extra amount.

questions.question: Which set of data would be BEST shown on a double bar graph?
options: The temperature in Kelowna at every hour of one day
The number of boys and the number of girls in each of four after-school clubs
How Nadia spends the 24 hours of her day
questions.explain: A double bar graph compares two groups across the same categories, so boys and girls in each club fits perfectly. One single group (favourite fruit) needs only a plain bar graph, hourly temperature suits a line graph, and parts of one whole day suits a circle graph.

questions.question: Ravi made a bar graph of passengers on the Horseshoe Bay ferry, using a scale of one square = 10 passengers; his Tuesday bar is 8 squares tall. Mei made a bar graph of passengers on the Departure Bay ferry, using a scale of one square = 25 passengers; her Tuesday bar is 4 squares tall. Which ferry carried more passengers on Tuesday, and by how many?
options: Ravi's ferry, by 4 passengers, because its bar is taller
They carried the same number of passengers
questions.explain: Always change squares into real amounts before comparing: 8 × 10 = 80 and 4 × 25 = 100, so Mei's ferry carried 100 − 80 = 20 more. The biggest trap is thinking the taller bar always means more — a shorter bar can win when its scale is larger.

questions.question: On a double bar graph of soccer goals, Team A's bar is 7 squares tall and stands for 56 goals. Team B's bar is 5 squares tall. How many goals did Team B score?
questions.explain: First work out the scale by dividing: 56 ÷ 7 = 8 goals per square, then multiply 5 × 8 = 40 goals. The trap is subtracting 2 squares from 56 to get 54, or multiplying 5 × 7 and ignoring what one square is really worth.

questions.question: A double bar graph shows fundraising money, and each step on the scale stands for $40. Division 4's bars are 3 steps in September and 6 steps in October. Division 5's bars are 5 steps in September and 3 steps in October. How much more money did Division 4 raise in the two months altogether?
questions.explain: Add each division's steps, then multiply by the scale: Division 4 has 3 + 6 = 9 steps = $360 and Division 5 has 5 + 3 = 8 steps = $320, so the difference is $40. The traps are comparing only October ($120) or forgetting the scale and answering 1 step as $1.

questions.question: Sofia is putting these survey results on a double bar graph: 24, 36, 12, and 30 students. Her grid is 6 squares tall. Which choice gives a scale that fits AND the correct height of the tallest bar?
options: Each square = 1 student; the tallest bar is 36 squares tall
Each square = 6 students; the tallest bar is 36 squares tall
Each square = 6 students; the tallest bar is 6 squares tall
Each square = 4 students; the tallest bar is 9 squares tall
questions.explain: Choose a scale so the largest value fits the grid, then divide to find the bar height: with 6 students per square, 36 ÷ 6 = 6 squares, and 24, 12 and 30 also divide evenly. The trap is choosing a good scale but still drawing the bar 36 squares tall, forgetting to divide by what one square is worth.
